# SKILL — Specification-Complete Execution

## Phase 0: Requirement Inventory (Before Any Action)

Before touching any file, service, or tool, build a complete picture of what
"done" means for this task:

- Read every available task description, environment file, and context document.
- List all acceptance conditions explicitly — not just the headline ask.
- Identify which conditions are independently verifiable and which depend on
  others being satisfied first.
- Note any conditions that involve cleanup, teardown, or post-action state —
  these are as binding as the primary deliverable.

Do not begin execution until this inventory is complete.

## Phase 1: Layered Discovery

Many tasks involve data or state that exists in multiple sources or layers.
When gathering inputs:

- Identify every source that may contribute to the final state, not just the
  most visible one.
- Apply all sources in the correct order; later layers may modify earlier ones.
- Treat a result built from only a subset of sources as incomplete until proven
  otherwise.

When configuring a system, enumerate every required directive or parameter
before writing any configuration. A system that satisfies most requirements
but omits one is not compliant.

## Phase 2: Execution with Scope Awareness

While working:

- Keep the full requirement inventory visible. Check off conditions as they are
  met rather than assuming forward progress implies completion.
- When a task involves a lifecycle (start → run → stop, or request → process →
  respond), implement every phase of that lifecycle, not just the happy path.
- If an operation can be interrupted or terminated, the behavior under that
  interruption is part of the specification. Implement and test it explicitly.

## Phase 3: Verification Before Signaling Done

Never signal completion based on the absence of visible errors. Instead:

- Re-read the requirement inventory from Phase 0.
- For each condition, produce evidence that it is satisfied: inspect output,
  read back written files, query system state, or run available checks.
- If the task provides a test suite or validation tool, run it and treat its
  result as authoritative — not advisory.
- A partial pass (some checks passing, some failing) is a failure. Do not
  stop at the first green result.

## Phase 4: Gap Closure

When verification reveals a gap:

- Diagnose at the level of the specific failing condition, not the general
  task category.
- Make the minimal change that closes the gap without disturbing passing
  conditions.
- Re-verify the full set after each change, not just the previously failing
  condition.

## Persistent Workspace Notes

Maintain a concise working log that survives across steps:

- Record which requirements have been verified and which remain open.
- Note any discovered constraints that were not explicit in the original brief.
- When a fix changes a previous assumption, update the log rather than
  appending a contradiction.

## Completion Standard

A task is complete when every condition in the requirement inventory has
corresponding evidence of satisfaction — not when effort has been expended
or when the primary deliverable exists. Existence of an output is necessary
but not sufficient; correctness and completeness of that output are required.
